title: Python Reference
description: A compact reference of the Python 3.13 syntax, built-in functions, methods and standard-library modules covered in the tutorial, grouped by topic with syntax and short examples.

entries.name: print()
entries.summary: Writes its arguments to the screen separated by sep (default a space) and followed by end (default a new line).
entries.syntax: print(*values, sep=" ", end="\n")

entries.name: input()
entries.summary: Shows a prompt, waits for the user to press Enter and returns the typed text as a string. Convert with int() or float() before doing arithmetic.
entries.syntax: text = input("Prompt: ")

entries.name: name = value
entries.summary: Creates or rebinds a variable; no type declaration is needed. Augmented forms such as += update in place, and several names can be assigned at once. A # starts a comment.
entries.syntax:
x = 1
x += 2
a, b = 1, 2   # comment
notes: Names use snake_case; UPPER_CASE signals a constant by convention only.
Assignment never copies a list or dict; both names refer to the same object.

entries.name: Indentation and blocks
entries.summary: A line ending with a colon opens a block; the indented lines below it (four spaces by convention) belong to that block.
notes: Mixing tabs and spaces raises TabError.
Inconsistent indentation raises IndentationError before the program runs.

entries.name: type() and isinstance()
entries.summary: type(value) returns the class of a value; isinstance(value, Class) tests whether a value is an instance of a class or its subclasses.
entries.syntax:
type(x)
isinstance(x, int)

entries.name: int(), float(), str(), bool()
entries.summary: Explicit conversions between the basic types. int() and float() parse text; str() formats anything; bool() applies truthiness.
entries.syntax: int("42")  float("2.5")  str(7)  bool(x)
notes: int("3.7") raises ValueError; use float() for decimals.

entries.name: Indexing and slicing
entries.summary: s[i] is the character at position i (negative counts from the end); s[start:stop:step] returns a substring up to but excluding stop. Works on lists and tuples too; len() gives the length.

example.code:
word = "Python"
print(word[0], word[-1], word[1:4], word[::-1])  # P n yth nohtyP

entries.name: strip(), upper(), lower(), title()
entries.summary: Return a new string with surrounding whitespace removed or the case changed. Strings are immutable, so assign the result.
entries.syntax: s.strip()  s.lstrip()  s.upper()  s.lower()  s.title()

entries.name: split() and join()
entries.summary: split() cuts a string into a list on whitespace or a separator; join() is called on the separator and glues an iterable of strings together.
entries.syntax: s.split()  s.split(",")  ", ".join(items)

entries.name: in, find(), replace(), startswith()
entries.summary: Test for a substring with in, get its position with find() (-1 if absent), swap text with replace(), test the ends with startswith() and endswith(), count occurrences with count().
entries.syntax: "py" in s  s.find("py")  s.replace(old, new)  s.startswith("http")  s.count("a")

entries.name: f-strings
entries.summary: A string prefixed with f evaluates expressions in braces and inserts them; a colon adds a format specification for decimals, width, alignment and separators.
entries.syntax: f"{value}"  f"{price:.2f}"  f"{n:,}"  f"{name:>10}"  f"{x!r}"

entries.summary: Addition, subtraction, multiplication, true division (always a float), floor division, remainder and power. ** groups from the right and binds tighter than unary minus.
notes: -7 // 2 is -4: floor division rounds towards negative infinity.

entries.name: round(), abs(), min(), max(), sum()
entries.summary: round(x, n) rounds to n decimals using banker's rounding for exact halves; abs() gives the magnitude; min(), max() and sum() work on any iterable and accept a key where it makes sense.
entries.syntax: round(2.675, 2)  abs(-3)  min(items)  max(items, key=len)  sum(items)
notes: divmod(17, 5) returns (3, 2), the quotient and remainder together.

entries.name: math module
entries.summary: Square roots, rounding up and down, constants and float comparison: sqrt(), floor(), ceil(), pi, isclose().
entries.syntax:
import math
math.sqrt(16)  math.floor(4.7)  math.ceil(4.2)  math.isclose(a, b)

entries.name: decimal.Decimal
entries.summary: Exact decimal arithmetic for money. Build Decimals from strings, never from floats, to avoid copying binary rounding errors.
entries.syntax:
from decimal import Decimal
Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2")

entries.name: random module
entries.summary: Pseudo-random numbers for games and sampling: randint() (both ends included), random(), choice(), shuffle(), sample(). seed() makes results repeatable.
entries.syntax:
import random
random.randint(1, 6)  random.choice(items)  random.seed(42)
notes: Use the secrets module, not random, for passwords and tokens.

entries.name: if / elif / else
entries.summary: Runs the first block whose condition is true; else catches the rest. The one-line form a if condition else b chooses between two values.

entries.name: == != < <= > >= in is
entries.summary: Equality, inequality and ordering comparisons return booleans; in tests membership; is tests identity and is used with None. Comparisons can be chained: 0 <= x < 10.
entries.syntax: a == b  a != b  x in items  value is None  18 <= age < 65

entries.name: and / or / not
entries.summary: Combine conditions. and and or evaluate lazily and return the deciding operand, which gives the default-value idiom name or "Anonymous".
entries.syntax: a and b   a or b   not a
notes: x == 1 or 2 is always true; write x == 1 or x == 2, or x in (1, 2).

entries.name: match / case
entries.summary: Structural pattern matching (Python 3.10+): compares a value against several patterns, binds captured names, and uses _ as the catch-all.
entries.syntax:
match value:
    case 200:
        ...
    case ["go", direction]:
        ...
    case _:
        ...

entries.name: for and while
entries.summary: for iterates over the items of any iterable; while repeats as long as a condition stays true. Both accept an else block that runs when the loop was not ended by break.
notes: A while loop must change something its condition depends on, or reach a break, to avoid running forever.

entries.name: range()
entries.summary: A lazy sequence of integers from start (default 0) up to but excluding stop, in steps of step (default 1, may be negative).
entries.syntax: range(stop)  range(start, stop)  range(start, stop, step)
notes: range(1, 10) stops at 9; use range(1, 11) for 1 to 10 inclusive.

entries.name: break and continue
entries.summary: break leaves the innermost loop immediately; continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves on to the next.

entries.name: enumerate() and zip()
entries.summary: enumerate() yields (index, item) pairs, with an optional start; zip() walks several sequences in parallel and stops at the shortest.
entries.syntax:
for i, item in enumerate(items, start=1):
for a, b in zip(list_a, list_b):

entries.name: list
entries.summary: An ordered, mutable sequence written in square brackets. Supports indexing, slicing, in, len() and loops. Assigning a list to a second name creates an alias; copy() makes an independent copy.
entries.syntax:
items = [1, 2, 3]
items[0]  items[-1]  items[1:3]  items.copy()

entries.name: append(), insert(), extend(), remove(), pop()
entries.summary: In-place list changes: add at the end, at a position or several at once; remove by value; remove and return by position. All return None except pop().
entries.syntax: items.append(x)  items.insert(0, x)  items.extend([a, b])  items.remove(x)  items.pop()
notes: numbers = numbers.sort() stores None; call sort() on its own line.

entries.name: sort() and sorted()
entries.summary: sort() reorders a list in place; sorted() returns a new sorted list from any iterable. Both accept reverse=True and a key function.
entries.syntax: items.sort()  sorted(items, key=len, reverse=True)

entries.name: tuple
entries.summary: An ordered, immutable sequence; a one-item tuple needs a trailing comma. Tuples unpack into variables and can be dict keys.
entries.syntax:
point = (3, 4)
x, y = point
single = (42,)

entries.name: set
entries.summary: An unordered collection of unique, hashable items with fast membership tests and set algebra: | union, & intersection, - difference, ^ symmetric difference.
entries.syntax:
tags = {"a", "b"}
tags.add(x)  tags.discard(x)  a | b  a & b  a - b
notes: {} is an empty dict; use set() for an empty set.

entries.name: dict
entries.summary: Maps hashable keys to values and preserves insertion order. Reading a missing key with [] raises KeyError.
entries.syntax:
user = {"name": "Ada"}
user["age"] = 36
del user["name"]
"age" in user

entries.name: get(), setdefault(), pop(), items(), update()
entries.summary: Safe reads with a default, insert-if-missing, remove and return, (key, value) pairs for loops, and merging another mapping.
entries.syntax: d.get(k, default)  d.setdefault(k, [])  d.pop(k, default)  d.items()  d.update(other)

entries.name: Comprehensions and generator expressions
entries.summary: Build a list, set or dict from an iterable in one expression, with an optional if filter. Parentheses instead of brackets give a lazy generator, ideal inside sum(), max(), any() and all().

entries.name: def / return
entries.summary: Defines a function with parameters; return hands back a value and ends the call. Without return the function returns None.
entries.syntax:
def name(param1, param2):
    return value

entries.name: Default and keyword arguments
entries.summary: Parameters with a default are optional; arguments can be passed by name in any order. Never use a mutable default such as [] or {}; use None and create it inside.
entries.syntax:
def book(guests, nights=1, breakfast=False):
book(2, breakfast=True)

entries.name: *args and **kwargs
entries.summary: *name collects extra positional arguments into a tuple and **name collects extra keyword arguments into a dict. In a call, * and ** unpack sequences and dicts into arguments.
entries.syntax:
def f(*args, **kwargs): ...
f(*items, **options)

entries.name: Docstrings, type hints and lambda
entries.summary: A string as the first statement documents a function and is shown by help(); annotations describe intended types without run-time enforcement. lambda defines a one-expression function, mostly as a sort key.
entries.syntax:
def area(w: float, h: float) -> float:
    """Return the area of a rectangle."""
    return w * h

sorted(people, key=lambda p: p["age"])

entries.name: import / from / as
entries.summary: Loads a module once and exposes its names: import the whole module, specific names, or rename with as. Avoid from module import *.
entries.syntax:
import math
from datetime import date
import numpy as np

entries.name: if __name__ == "__main__":
entries.summary: True only when the file is run directly, not when it is imported. Put script behaviour under it so the module stays importable.
entries.syntax:
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

entries.name: Packages
entries.summary: A folder of modules, conventionally with an __init__.py, imported with dotted names that follow the folder structure.
entries.syntax:
from geometry import units
from geometry.units import cm_to_inches
notes: Never name a file or folder after a standard-library module such as random or json.

entries.name: try / except
entries.summary: Runs the try block and jumps to the matching except block when an exception of that type (or a subclass) is raised. A tuple catches several types; as binds the exception object.
notes: A bare except: catches everything, including KeyboardInterrupt; name the exceptions you expect.

entries.name: else / finally
entries.summary: else runs only when the try block raised nothing; finally always runs, even after return or an unhandled exception, and is the place for clean-up.

entries.name: raise and custom exceptions
entries.summary: Signals an error from your own code with a built-in exception type and a message; a class derived from Exception lets callers catch your error specifically. A bare raise inside except re-raises.

entries.name: class, __init__ and self
entries.summary: class defines a type; __init__ initialises each new instance; self is the instance, passed automatically as the first argument of every method.

example.code:
ada = Account("Ada")
ada.deposit(50)   # same as Account.deposit(ada, 50)

entries.name: __repr__, __str__ and __eq__
entries.summary: Dunder methods that control how an object is shown to developers, printed to users and compared with ==.
entries.syntax:
def __repr__(self): return f"Point({self.x}, {self.y})"
def __str__(self): ...
def __eq__(self, other): ...

entries.name: Inheritance and super()
entries.summary: class Child(Parent) inherits the parent's methods and may override them; super().__init__() runs the parent's initialiser.

entries.name: @dataclass
entries.summary: Generates __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ from annotated fields. Use field(default_factory=list) for mutable defaults.

entries.name: open() and with
entries.summary: Opens a file in a mode with an explicit encoding; the with statement closes it automatically, even when an exception occurs. Loop over the file object to read it line by line.
entries.syntax:
with open("notes.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("text\n")

with open("notes.txt", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    for line in file:
        print(line.rstrip())

entries.name: File modes
entries.summary: "r" read (default), "w" write and truncate, "a" append, "x" create only, "rb"/"wb" binary, "r+" read and write.
entries.syntax: open(path, "r")  open(path, "a")  open(path, "rb")
notes: "w" empties an existing file the moment it is opened.

entries.name: pathlib.Path
entries.summary: Object-oriented paths: join with /, test with exists(), create folders with mkdir(), list with glob(), and read or write text in one call.
entries.syntax:
from pathlib import Path
p = Path("data") / "notes.txt"
p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")  p.write_text("...", encoding="utf-8")

entries.name: csv module
entries.summary: Reads and writes comma-separated files with correct quoting; DictReader and DictWriter map rows to dictionaries keyed by the header. Open CSV files with newline="".

entries.name: json.dumps(), loads(), dump(), load()
entries.summary: Convert Python data to a JSON string and back; the versions without s work with an open file object or HTTP response instead of a string. indent and sort_keys make output readable and stable.
entries.syntax:
json.dumps(data, indent=2)  json.loads(text)
json.dump(data, file, indent=2)  json.load(file)

example.code:
import json
print(json.dumps({"ok": True, "n": None}))   # {"ok": true, "n": null}

notes: load() takes a file object, not a path; loads() takes a string.

entries.name: urllib.request.urlopen()
entries.summary: Fetches a URL from the standard library and returns a response object with status, headers and a readable body. Catch HTTPError before URLError and always pass a timeout.
entries.syntax:
from urllib.request import urlopen
with urlopen(url, timeout=10) as response:
    data = json.load(response)

entries.name: python -m venv
entries.summary: Creates an isolated environment in a folder; activate it with source .venv/bin/activate (macOS, Linux) or .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 (Windows PowerShell), leave with deactivate.
entries.syntax: python -m venv .venv

entries.name: pip
entries.summary: Installs packages from PyPI into the active environment. Run it as python -m pip; freeze writes the exact installed versions for requirements.txt.
entries.syntax:
python -m pip install requests
python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
